threat_assessment:
Five colours and a tutor on a stick. The table files you as archenemy before you untap, and the four Game Changers named in the pregame seal it. Let them. They are watching the wrong object.

Sisay lands on turn three in ninety-five games out of a hundred, so stop treating her arrival as the milestone — she is your floor, not your plan. What you do in the two turns after her is the whole deck.

With no other legend out she is a 2/2 and the gate reads "cheaper than two." Three cards in the list are legal there, one of them adds no colour, and there are no legendary lands sitting under that gate. Never activate into a cold board — put a colour-diverse legend down first and fire next turn.

Count colours among your other legends, never mana. One colour opens ten targets and two opens twenty-three, so buy that second colour early and buy it cheap. Katilda, Kinnan, Lotho and Saffi are each two mana for two colours — thirteen more cards of access on something that looks like a draft creature.

Then stop at four. Three colours opens twenty-eight and four opens all thirty-three, and the fifth opens nothing at all, because nothing in this deck costs more than five. Spend that turn holding protection instead of chasing a rung that pays you zero.

Now learn the bill, because it is only five cards wide. Exactly five cards here carry {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}: Sisay's activation, Najeela's activation, Jodah's cost and Esika's cost all spend it, and only Jegantha adds it. Four spend, one produces — check that register before you tap anything.

Jegantha is the trap inside her own solution. She costs five, so she is legal only at power six, which means four colours are already on the board and you can probably pay without her. Fix your mana early or draw it, and treat Jegantha as a payoff rather than a fix.

Black decides whether you activate at all: twenty-one sources against a target of thirty-six, and a 61% on-curve rate even counting rocks and dorks, against 94% white and 95% green. When a fetchland gives you a choice, take black. When black is coming off one permanent, deploy the second source before you make the greedy fetch.

Four things flip you from ignored to archenemy. Five untapped sources covering all five colours beside an untapped Sisay. A body that visibly solves the bill — Jegantha, Bloom Tender, Faeburrow Elder, Esika. Najeela. And a second activation inside one turn cycle, which ends the conversation.

Choose which of those you show, and on which turn. Do not let draw order choose for you.

Sequence your colours onto bodies nobody fears. Katilda, Kinnan, Lotho, Kambal, Kutzil and Saffi each buy two rungs and frighten no one. Leave Najeela and Jodah in the library, where they are safe and still yours — your deflection budget spends down every time the engine shows itself (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection).

Do not bluff with open mana. Five visible colours advertise interaction you structurally do not have: every counterspell and both free protection instants sit inside the twenty-six cards Sisay can never reach. Hold what is real; otherwise tap out behind a modest permanent and look poorer than you are.

Here is the asymmetry the rest of the table does not get. Your scariest cards live in your library and you reach them at will, so you never need Najeela in hand and never have to look like you have her. Play the whole midgame as a fair legends deck and time the tell to the turn it wins, not the turn it impresses.

Rhystic Study is the tell you did not choose. It is a Game Changer, it is non-legendary, and it will make you archenemy faster than anything Sisay can find. At a table still deciding who to hit, sit on it a turn.

Learn how the good pilots kill you, because it changes your sequencing today. They do not spend removal on Sisay — they kill the rung, the one legend supplying a colour, in response to the activation, so your power drops and the fetch shrinks under you. Audit single-sourced colours every turn, deploy the redundant one before the greedy fetch, and go get Shalai the moment she is legal.

A sweeper is the other way you die, and it charges you twice: the board, and the ladder from twenty-eight targets back to three. That one has its own instructions below.

When you do embrace the label, embrace it on the verified line. Stack 002 makes Najeela with Derevi a deterministic, unbounded combat loop, and it names exactly what you must bring: five colours untapped before the first combat, both creatures surviving, and damage getting through to a player. Stop waiting for a wide board — the loop grows its own, three attackers in the first combat and five in the second.

Hold the break-even combat in your head, not the card count. Combat one is funded from your lands, combat two breaks exactly even at five untap triggers against five mana, and combat three onward runs a surplus that never closes. Present it only on a turn you can pay that first five.

Route the payment through Command Tower and Plaza of Heroes' any-colour-among-legendary-permanents mode and the loop costs you zero life — leave City of Brass and Mana Confluence untapped rather than tapping all five out of habit. Then count their untapped creatures before you swing, because Derevi has to connect and one well-timed blocker in the first combat is the entire answer.

Notice what the register means on that turn: the loop re-buys the same five pips Sisay's activation wants. One resource gates both, so the turn you present Najeela is a turn you stop fetching. Decide which you are doing before you untap.

Take the archenemy seat on purpose — three colours down, five pips genuinely payable, protection up or Kutzil holding your window open — and take it on your turn. Until that turn, be the fourth most interesting board at the table and enjoy it. You know what you are building toward and they are guessing.

One thing stays open on purpose. Whether a legend you just fetched can help pay for the next activation on the same turn is unsettled — the resolution that asked failed its check. Plan on one activation per turn cycle; a chain is a gift, not a plan.
matchups:
Sweeper control. Assume the wrath — across four players one is close to certain — and price it double, because against you it takes the board and drops the ladder from twenty-eight targets to three. So keep a two-colour legend in HAND rather than on board. Katilda, Kinnan, Lotho, Saffi, Kambal, Kutzil: the hand copy rebuilds two rungs, the board copy dies with everything else.

Know which of your saves actually save. Flawless Maneuver, Heroic Intervention and Boros Charm's indestructible mode beat destruction wraths and do precisely nothing against exile or against a -X/-X like your own Toxic Deluge. Read their deck, then choose which save you are holding for.

Protection is available by turn six in eighty games out of a hundred and arrives on turn two on average, so play as though you have it. Fetch into that number instead of sandbagging for a save you probably already hold.

Deluge is your permission slip. You recover from a wipe cheaper than anyone at the table, so pick the timing yourself rather than letting the control seat pick it (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). Rebuild worst threat first, and count the extra two mana each trip through the command zone charges you before you promise yourself a recast (strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance).

Stax and tax. You are the beatdown here and you do not get to argue about it — race the lock's completion, because you never own the long game underneath one (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Five coloured pips with zero generic, activated every turn, is the most tax-exposed shape in the format. Recount your activations under the tax, not your cards.

Recount honestly, because three of your own accelerants quit on you. Delighted Halfling makes mana for legendary spells and an activation is not a spell; Unclaimed Territory is creature spells only; Sol Ring is colourless against five coloured pips. Stop counting all three toward the activation.

Two read the other way once you read the clause instead of the phrase. Plaza of Heroes' any-colour-among-legendary-permanents mode carries no restriction at all, and Secluded Courtyard's own text says "or activate an ability" — Sisay is a Human Soldier, so name Human and it pays her. Katilda is the sleeper: she hands Human creatures a mana ability, which turns your commander into a white source.

Name your out before you go get it. Loran is three mana, live from the second colour onward, and destroys the artifact or enchantment as she enters; Teferi's minus is the backup. Fetch the piece locking YOU, not the scariest piece on the table (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial).

Aggro. You are behind roughly 120 life spread across three defences, and the goldfish has you at four bodies on turn six — so do not race, and do not pretend the board is your answer. Buy virtual answers instead of spending real ones.

Thalia makes their creatures and nonbasic lands enter tapped, Sheoldred bills them two life a draw, Shalai hands you and your other creatures hexproof, and Flowering turns every legend into a warded body. All four are legendary at two to four mana, so all four are one activation away from the second colour onward (strategy:card-advantage.virtual).

That is the whole trick against three attackers. One fetch that blanks plans at three seats beats one removal spell that answers one card. If a single seat drags you into a race, treat it as a subgame, spend the minimum that wins it, and keep your eyes on the other two (strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry).

Know your blind classes before you promise yourself an answer. This deck answers creatures, artifacts and enchantments, and answers neither graveyards nor lands. Do not hold a fetch for a problem you cannot fetch for — tax it instead.

Combo. Invert everything. Hold the pips for interaction and count the table's open mana rather than climbing, because a wide gate is worth nothing if the game ends before you walk through it (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). Your one Path to Exile is worth most the moment the piece hits the battlefield — spend it there, not on the turn you finally feel safe (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy).

The structural problem is that your interaction is exactly what Sisay cannot see. All six counterspells, Fierce Guardianship, Flawless Maneuver, Drannith Magistrate and Grand Abolisher sit inside the twenty-six cards outside her reach, so they arrive by draw or not at all. Mulligan for enablers and disruption here, never for payoffs.

Fetch disruption rather than a finisher. Teferi pushes them to sorcery speed and Kutzil switches their spells off during your turn outright. Take either over Najeela for as long as a combo deck is alive.

Fair value midrange. Here you are cleanly the control seat, so slow the game down and stop hunting for action. Picture turn fifteen with everybody on their best draws — you like that picture, which means your job is making the game reach it (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock). Look boring for a turn or two after every visible fetch and sequence Najeela and Jodah last (strategy:multiplayer.pod-management).

Graveyard hate. Mostly a blank against you, and every Bojuka Bog pointed here instead of at the reanimator seat is a card you got for free — say nothing and let them spend it. Do not build a plan on your own yard either: Saffi's sacrifice trigger is the entire recursion suite. Keep Dauthi Voidwalker for those decks, and remember he arrives by draw like everything else non-legendary.

Every archetype above ends at the same instruction. Fetch the card that changes what the table is allowed to do, and leave the card that ends the game in the library until the turn it ends it.

The one line here that has been walked through the rules and survived an adversarial check is Najeela with Derevi, and it wants five colours payable before the first combat and again every combat after. Build toward that mana, not toward the nine lines the combo data flags but nobody has resolved. Stumble into those. Never keep a hand for them.

cover.tagline: The tutor that widens every time it fires - and the five-pip bill that comes due every time.
cover.identity: Sisay, Weatherlight Captain is a repeatable battlefield tutor whose reach is bought in colours: she is a 2/2 plus one for each colour among your other legendary permanents, and {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} searches out any legendary permanent with mana value strictly less than her power. That makes this an access curve rather than a card curve - 3 legal targets at power 2, then 10, 23, 28 and 33 as the board picks up colours - funded by 40 lands and a small battery of bodies that can produce five distinct coloured pips at once. It is a bracket 4 (Optimized) list on contents alone: four Game Changers put the floor there independently of any combo line, and the Najeela combat loop is the closer.

how_it_wins:
Five colours, a tutor commander and forty lands: the table has you filed as a greedy pile before you untap. Let them file. What is actually sitting across from them is a fair {2}{W} creature with no tap symbol on her ability and no once-per-turn clause anywhere on the card, in a deck whose only real currency is access.

Read her power, never her mana cost. She is a 2/2 plus one for every colour among your OTHER legendary permanents, and she finds any legendary permanent cheaper than that power. Zero colours is three legal targets. One colour is ten. Two colours is twenty-three. So the move is never "cast Sisay, activate Sisay" — put a colour-dense legend down first and activate second.

Play toward the second colour, then stop climbing at four. One colour to two is thirteen new targets, the largest step on the ladder, and it is the step that first makes Najeela legal. Four colours already opens all 33, because nothing in this list costs more than five. The fifth colour buys combat stats and no access at all — spend that turn holding up protection instead.

Now the bill, because it is where new pilots die. Four cards here demand {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} and exactly one — Jegantha — adds it. Sol Ring makes colourless, Delighted Halfling's coloured mana is for legendary spells only, Unclaimed Territory is creature spells only. Use those three to deploy her a turn early, then pay her with the six that can: Bloom Tender, Faeburrow Elder, Jegantha, Esika, Relic of Legends, Selvala.

Stop mulliganing for the captain. Ten thousand seeded games put her on the battlefield on turn three in 8,028 of them and by turn six in 99 of every 100. The assembly that actually gates you — Sisay plus a multi-colour mana body — arrives by turn six a little over half the time, so keep the fuel and let her go and find the payoffs.

Your removal is a shopping list, not a card in hand. One unconditional creature answer and one sweeper is the whole suite, because Thalia makes their creatures and nonbasic lands enter tapped, Teferi and Kutzil take away the turns they are allowed to act on, and Kambal and Sheoldred bill them for their own spells and draws. Every one of them is legendary at mana value 2 to 4. Go and get the tax that hurts the seat that is beating you, not the scariest one.

Then close with Najeela. She plus Derevi is the one line here that has been walked against the Comprehensive Rules and cleared an adversarial check: an unbounded combat loop that ends the table and costs you nothing in life. It is not free in mana — it re-buys five colours every single combat and needs five of your creatures connecting. Present it on the turn the base can pay that toll, never on the turn the fetch would look impressive.

And know the hole you cannot patch. Twenty-six of your nonland cards are not legendary, so she will never see them: three of the six cards that pay her, every counterspell, both free protection spells and all four Game Changers. She finds payoffs. Fuel you draw.

card_roles.Sisay, Weatherlight Captain: Count colours before you count mana: she is 2/2 plus one for every colour among your other legendary permanents, and she finds any legendary permanent cheaper than that power. No tap symbol and no once-per-turn line, so the only ceiling on her is how often you can raise {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}.
card_roles.An Offer You Can't Refuse: One blue mana to stop the wrath or the exile aimed at your ladder. The two Treasures you hand back cost less than rebuilding four rungs — spend it on the spell that takes your board, not the one that annoys you.
card_roles.Arcane Denial: Two mana to keep an activation alive, and you replace the card on the next upkeep. Point it at whatever would cost you the most colours.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any colour in the identity for two mana, which makes it one of the few rocks that pays a real pip of her bill. Play it ahead of a three-drop, never after.
card_roles.Birds of Paradise: A one-mana source of any colour, which is the best turn-one card a deck needing five different colours can have. Treat it as a land and protect it like one.
card_roles.Bloom Tender: One mana for each colour among your permanents, so it scales with the ladder you are already climbing. Four colours on board and it pays four of her five pips by itself.
card_roles.Boros Charm: Indestructible for every permanent you control is the mode you keep it for; the four damage is a footnote. Hold it the moment a red or black seat is one card away from a sweeper.
card_roles.Bristly Bill, Spine Sower: A green rung for two mana that turns each land drop into a counter. Fetch him early because green is missing, not late because the pump is nice.
card_roles.Dauthi Voidwalker: Double black on turn two is why black carries the highest source target in the deck — cast him on curve when you can, and let the exile clause shut a graveyard seat off. Not legendary, so she will never hand him to you.
card_roles.Delighted Halfling: Deploy her a turn early and uncounterable, then stop counting it: the coloured mana is for legendary spells only and buys none of her activation. Excellent first drop, false friend from turn three onward.
card_roles.Derevi, Empyrial Tactician: Three rungs on one three-mana body, the biggest single climb in the deck, plus an untap trigger every time one of your creatures connects. He is also the quiet half of the kill — never trade him off casually.
card_roles.Dihada, Binder of Wills: Three rungs and a four-card dig for legends with Treasures attached. Remember the +2 as a protection button: vigilance, lifelink and indestructible on the captain until your next turn.
card_roles.Dispel: One mana for the instant that would blow you out mid-activation. Keep it up against the combo seat and ship it from any opener that has one land.
card_roles.Drannith Magistrate: Shuts off every command zone, graveyard and exile cast at the table at once. You have to draw him — she cannot see a nonlegendary body.
card_roles.Emiel the Blessed: Three mana a blink, so spend it on the enter-the-battlefield value you actually need, or to save a mana dork from a removal spell. The loops he appears in have no passing stack; play the value, not the promise.
card_roles.Esika, God of the Tree // The Prismatic: One mana of any colour, and she grants that same ability to every other legendary creature you control — the board you fetched becomes fuel for the next fetch. On the battlefield she is green only, so count one rung, not five.
card_roles.Esper Sentinel: A white one-drop that taxes their first noncreature spell every turn, and the ladder pumps the tax as it grows. Cast it turn one and forget about it.
card_roles.Faeburrow Elder: One mana per colour among your permanents, and it grows with them. Both Vivid dorks are cards she cannot fetch, so if you want them you draw them.
card_roles.Fellwar Stone: Two mana for whatever colours the table's lands can produce, which in a four-player pod is usually the colour you are short. Expect less from it against a mono-colour seat.
card_roles.Fierce Guardianship: Free while you control a commander, so hold it on the turn you tap out to climb. It is the answer to the removal spell pointed at her and to the counterspell pointed at your fetch.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free indestructible for your whole board on the turn a sweeper resolves — the cheapest way to keep four rungs instead of restarting from three legal targets.
card_roles.Flowering of the White Tree: Ward {1} on every legend you control makes cheap removal miss the captain, and the +2/+1 is another point of her power. At two mana it is the cheapest insurance she can fetch for herself.
card_roles.Grand Abolisher: During your turn they cannot cast spells or activate their artifacts, creatures and enchantments. That is the window you climb three rungs in — but you have to draw him.
card_roles.Heliod, Sun-Crowned: An indestructible white rung that hands out lifelink for two mana and turns every life gain into a counter. Legal to fetch at power 4.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana, hexproof and indestructible for everything you own. It beats a targeted-removal turn and a wrath with the same card, so hold it rather than jam it.
card_roles.Ioreth of the Healing House: Untaps two other legendary creatures, which here means two more taps out of the pip battery. Fetch her once the mana bodies are already down, not before.
card_roles.Jegantha, the Wellspring: The only card in the deck that adds all five colours off a single tap — and at mana value 5 she is legal to fetch only once four colours are already out. Treat her as the payoff, never as the fix.
card_roles.Jodah, the Unifier: Five distinct pips to cast, the biggest anthem in the deck, and a free legendary spell every time you cast one from hand. He is the ceiling target: power 6 or nothing.
card_roles.Kambal, Consul of Allocation: Two rungs at three mana and a bill on every noncreature spell the table casts. Against a spell-heavy seat he is your removal suite.
card_roles.Katilda, Dawnhart Prime: Two rungs for two mana, and every Human you control taps for mana — the captain included. One of the best turn-two plays in the deck.
card_roles.Kenrith, the Returned King: Five modes on one white body, so fetch him when you already have mana and need whichever thing the board is missing. Reachable only at power 6.
card_roles.Kinnan, Bonder Prodigy: Two rungs for two mana, and every nonland permanent you tap for mana produces one extra — a whole additional pip out of Bloom Tender or Jegantha.
card_roles.Kodama of the West Tree: A green rung whose modified creatures fetch you a basic land on damage, with trample attached. It matters more than it reads in a deck that makes counters.
card_roles.Kutzil, Malamet Exemplar: Two rungs at three mana, and your opponents cannot cast spells during your turn. Buy that window before you present the kill, not after.
card_roles.Loran of the Third Path: Your only fetchable answer to an artifact or an enchantment, and she draws you a card every turn afterward. Go and get her the moment a lock piece lands.
card_roles.Lotho, Corrupt Shirriff: Two rungs for two mana, and every second spell any player casts hands you a Treasure. That Treasure pays a real coloured pip, which most of your acceleration does not.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Lunarch: One of only three cards legal at her base power, and the one that grows the rest of the board. Cast him with X when you can — whether a fetched copy survives with no X chosen is an open question on the record.
card_roles.Mox Amber: Free, legal at her base power, and it makes a colour only if a legendary creature or planeswalker is already out. It is the cold-start fetch that adds no rung by itself, so play a legend first.
card_roles.Najeela, the Blade-Blossom: Your red rung at three mana and half of the verified kill. Fetch her on the turn you can pay {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} in combat with five creatures able to connect — any earlier and you have simply told the table whom to kill.
card_roles.Negate: Two mana for the wrath, the lock piece or the removal aimed at your commander. Not legendary, so it arrives by draw and never by fetch.
card_roles.Path to Exile: One mana, exile, instant speed — the only unconditional creature answer in the deck. Spend it on the creature that ends the game, not the one that is merely large.
card_roles.Raff Capashen, Ship's Mage: Two rungs, and every legendary spell you own gains flash. Deploy the ladder on their end step, then untap with the mana up for her activation.
card_roles.Reki, the History of Kamigawa: A green rung that draws a card for every legendary spell you cast — the closest thing to a draw engine she can fetch for you.
card_roles.Relic of Legends: Any colour, and it taps your untapped legendary creatures for more of the same. One of the six pieces that genuinely pays her bill, and one of the three of those you have to draw.
card_roles.Rhystic Study: They pay or you draw, and this deck's card advantage sits at 7 against a budget of 10 — so resolve it as early as the mana allows. She will never find it for you.
card_roles.Rona, Herald of Invasion // Rona, Tolari: A blue rung at two mana that untaps whenever you cast a legendary spell, with looting attached. She is blue only on the front face — count one rung, not two.
card_roles.Saffi Eriksdotter: Two rungs for two mana and a sacrifice that returns a dying creature. Hold her over whichever body is currently paying your pips.
card_roles.Samut, Voice of Dissent: Flash, haste for the team, and a {W} untap every turn. She is legal only at power 6, so she tends to be the last rung rather than a step toward it.
card_roles.Seedborn Muse: Untaps everything during every opponent's untap step — three extra activation windows per turn cycle at a four-player table. Not legendary, so you draw her or you play without her.
card_roles.Selvala, Heart of the Wilds: X mana in any combination of colours for the greatest power among your creatures, which is frequently the captain herself. The fetchable half of the pip battery, legal at power 4.
card_roles.Shalai, Voice of Plenty: Hexproof for you and every other creature you control, on a body she can fetch at power 5. This is the answer to a targeted-removal seat that you can go and get.
card_roles.Sheoldred, the Apocalypse: A rung in your scarcest colour at four mana, plus two life off every card an opponent draws. Fetch her against the seat whose plan is drawing cards.
card_roles.Silence: One mana buys their entire turn. Save it for the turn you present the loop rather than spending it on a wrath you could have taken.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colourless on turn one, which deploys the captain a turn early and pays nothing toward her activation. Take the speed — then remember it made no colour.
card_roles.Surrak Dragonclaw: Three rungs on one body, flash, and your creature spells cannot be countered. A late rung at power 6, and the one that beats a blue seat.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana against a wrath, a counterspell or a combo instant. The 2/2 Bird they get is cheap next to the turn you would have spent rebuilding.
card_roles.Teferi, Time Raveler: Two rungs on a planeswalker, and while he lives the table may only act at sorcery speed — that is an activation window with no counterspell in it. His −3 bounces an artifact, creature or enchantment and replaces itself.
card_roles.Thalia, Heretic Cathar: A white rung that makes their creatures and nonbasic lands enter tapped — a turn of tempo taken from three seats with one card. One of the first taxes to go and fetch.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: Your only sweeper, and you choose both X and the turn. You rebuild from a wipe cheaper than the rest of the table does, so do not hold it waiting for perfect.
card_roles.Yoshimaru, Ever Faithful: A white rung for one mana that grows with every legendary permanent that follows it. Legal at her base power, which makes him a live fetch on the cold-start turn.

mulligan:
Everyone at this table mulligans hunting for the commander, and she is the single card in the deck you do not need to find — turn-three Sisay in 8,028 games out of 10,000. Keep for the things she cannot go and get.

That is one judgement, and you make it twice a game. Six cards in the 99 can pay her five-pip activation and three of them are not legendary, so those three only ever arrive off the top of your library. Fuel and colours in the opener; payoffs later, from the battlefield, for free.

A keep is three things. Two to four lands including at least one that makes any colour — Command Tower, City of Brass, Mana Confluence, Exotic Orchard, Forbidden Orchard, any fetch, or Secluded Courtyard named on Human. Something that accelerates and pays a coloured pip: Birds of Paradise, Bloom Tender, Faeburrow Elder, Arcane Signet, Fellwar Stone, Relic of Legends. And a cheap multicolour legend, which is what turns a hand that casts her into a hand that climbs.

Katilda, Kinnan, Lotho and Saffi each buy two rungs for two mana; Derevi buys three for three. A seven with one of those and one any-colour source is a snap keep — stop deliberating and shuffle up.

Ship the payoff hand on sight. Jodah, Kenrith, Surrak and Samut over two lands is four cards you cannot cast in front of a 2/2 whose entire menu is Mox Amber, Mikaeus and Yoshimaru — and she could have fetched every one of those legends herself.

Ship the fast hand that pays nothing. Sol Ring plus Delighted Halfling deploys her a turn early and covers not one pip of what she does next. That is the trap keep in this deck, and it looks like your best opener right up until you tap out.

Ship counterspells on one land. Interaction is the half of this list you draw into comfortably, and protection is already available by turn six in 80 games out of 100 — you are not the hand that has to hold the answer on turn one.

Two habits to take into game one. An early accelerant shows up by turn six in only 64 games out of 100, so a seven that already has one is ahead of your own curve — weight it heavily. And count colours rather than lands when the hand is close: you keep 84.2% of first sevens on the land rule alone, so lands were never the question.
upgrades:
Five cards in the 99 carry the string {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}. Four of them spend it and exactly one, Jegantha, adds it, so the deck buys one activation a turn. Six of the ten below are here to buy a second.

Those six split three and three, and the halves fail differently. Intruder Alarm, Marvin, Murderous Mimic and Freed from the Real untap a body you already control — Bloom Tender, Faeburrow Elder, Relic of Legends, Jegantha — so they need a board first. Cryptolith Rite, Chromatic Lantern and Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth change what your existing permanents produce, which is the half that works on an empty-ish table.

The access ladder is 3 / 10 / 23 / 28 / 33 legal fetch targets at zero through four colours among your other legends. The step being bought is one colour to two: +13 targets, better than double, and the rung where a mana-value-3 legend first comes into reach. A fifth colour adds zero new targets, so the ladder stops paying before the mana does.

Three of the ten are cards the commander can go and get instead of cards you draw. Marvin is mana value 2 and legal one colour in; Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose is 3 and legal two colours in; Urborg is 0 and legal at base power. That last one is the loud number — the deck runs zero legendary lands, so at base power the whole legal menu is three cards, and Urborg is a fourth.

Black is the thin colour: 21 total sources against a 36-source yardstick, while every other colour is asked for 22, and only 12 of the 21 are lands. Urborg and Chromatic Lantern both answer that by changing what the 40 land copies are rather than adding one more card that taps for a pip. Neither will move the colour-sources axis, because the manabase maths counts sources per card and models no static grant. The number staying put is a limit of the instrument, not a verdict on the cards.

One line in this deck carries a passing checker verdict — stack 002, the Najeela combat loop — and it re-buys {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} every combat. The deck can afford that toll about once. Bear Umbra is the only pick aimed at the toll rather than at the first payment, and its case is the timing: the untap rides an attack trigger, before the bill is due. The file is candid that two other cards hold the same two-card record against that toll and that this is one slot, not three.

Two picks move a counted axis. Beast Within takes interaction-breadth from 3 classes to 4, land 0 to 1 — land being the one permanent class nothing in the 99 answers. Vito takes threat-density 3 to 4 at mana value 3. Walking Ballista moves neither count, carries no wincon role at all, and is here as a second kill that shares nothing with the combat loop.

Adoption spans two orders of magnitude — Beast Within at EDHREC rank 25, Urborg at 73 and Chromatic Lantern at 84, out to Freed from the Real at 1,594 and Intruder Alarm at 1,720 — and the bracket column is flat at 4 before and 4 after on all ten. Read the tail as shape, not as quality. Four of the ten name a natural cut and six do not, which is the file telling you where it is confident about a trade and where it is only confident about a card.

Every combo line attached to these names is stamped "needs a stack scenario". Ten lines are fully contained in this deck already and four of those are two-card infinites, and none of them is verified either — so this list is candidates, sized honestly.

The obsolescence index is no help here, and how it fails is the useful part. Over this deck's two Vivid dorks it proposes ten replacements at similarities from 0.942 to 0.9755, and the advantages it lists are cost, power, toughness and flying — not one entry mentions mana. It also offers Sol Ring over Fellwar Stone at 0.9746, trading a coloured source for two colourless ones in a deck that runs both. The index measures similarity. This deck is buying colours.
mana_base:
Forty land copies across thirty-nine entries, and seventeen of them carry a tapped clause — 42% against the one-in-three budget the builder allows itself. The interesting figure is the one underneath: zero of them enter tapped unconditionally. Nine are shocks, tapped only if you decline to pay two life. The other eight read "unless you have two or more opponents", which at a four-player table is not a tapped land at all.

Where pip share and source share disagree, they disagree on purpose. White carries 38.3% of the deck's pips on 23.1% of its sources; red carries 8.0% of the pips on 18.5% of the sources. In most lists that gap is a misallocation. Here the cost that runs the deck asks for one of every colour, so the base is levelled rather than tuned — 27 green, 26 white, 22 blue, 21 black, 21 red, a spread of six across the whole rainbow.

Black is the exception, and it carries a target of its own: 36 sources against 22 for the other four. It is the one colour where a meaningful share of the cards want two pips rather than one — Dauthi Voidwalker's double black on turn two, Sheoldred's at four — so the target sizes for two black sources by turn three. Twelve black lands gets there on curve 29.9% of the time. Every other colour lands between 70.4% and 78.7% on lands alone.

Nine dorks and five rocks are what close that gap. Counted in, black rises to 21 sources and 61.0%, and the rest go to 89.5% red, 90.7% blue, 94.4% white, 95.1% green. It is why the audit's verdict of 17 ramp pieces against a 10–12 budget reads as fixing rather than speed: the creature half of this mana base is the colour-fixing, and Bloom Tender and Faeburrow Elder are load-bearing lands with legs.

One accounting rule decides more here than anywhere else. A source whose text says "spend this mana only" counts for nothing unless the clause reaches abilities — so Delighted Halfling and Unclaimed Territory are zeroed, while Plaza of Heroes keeps an unrestricted coloured mode and Secluded Courtyard's clause says "or activate an ability", and both count. Raw mana crosses five on turn six at a mean of 5.869, against 3.187 on turn three. From six onward the question stops being how much and starts being which.

combo_lines.002:
The clause this case turns on is CR 508.4: “Such creatures are ‘attacking’ but, for the purposes of trigger events and effects, they never ‘attacked.’” Najeela's tokens arrive tapped and attacking. They deal damage, they get untapped, they can be declared next combat — and they are invisible to the trigger that made them. The loop therefore grows between combats and never inside one.

Two citations carry the arithmetic. CR 603.2c, “However, it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences”, gives Derevi one untap trigger per creature that connects rather than one per damage event, so triggers equal attackers while the activation cost stays fixed at five. Attackers then follow 2A − 1: three, five, nine, seventeen, thirty-three. Combat 1 comes up two triggers short and must be funded from outside. Combat 2 is exact. Combat 3 runs a surplus of four.

On the life cost the record corrects the popular telling. CR 118.3c: “Activating mana abilities is not mandatory, even if paying a cost is.” Nothing compels a tap of City of Brass or Mana Confluence, and Command Tower plus Plaza of Heroes cover all five colours between them, so the floor is zero life per combat.

One further exhibit, because it is the step at which the line could have died. CR 506.4 lists the causes of removal from combat exhaustively, and a defending player leaving the game is not among them. The seventeen attackers stay in combat, and the army is free to be declared at the next seat.

The holding: real, deterministic, unbounded — and not a two-card infinite. These two cards produce no mana between them. A base capable of {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} every combat, and five creatures connecting, are requirements of the line rather than conveniences of the board it was tested on. On the nine other combo records this deck contains, the record is silent.
